1:
Its brevity is remarked first. Clarke calls it the shortest psalm in the collection, notes that thirty-two manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi write it as part of the psalm before it, and that one of Kennicott's and two of De Rossi's omit it altogether. He takes it to celebrate the redemption from the Babylonish captivity as the grand type of the world's redemption by Christ, and reports the Syriac heading, that it was spoken concerning Ananias and his followers coming out of the furnace, though it also foretells the vocation of the Gentiles. Henry passes on a Jewish fancy that turns the shortness into doctrine: it consists of two verses to signify that in the days of the Messiah God should be glorified by two sorts of people — Jews by the law of Moses and Gentiles by the seven precepts of the sons of Noah — which yet make one church, as these two verses make one psalm.

That Paul settles its sense they take for granted. Henry says the apostle has furnished us with a key, quoting it as proof that the gospel was to be preached to and entertained by the Gentile nations, which was so great a stumbling-block to them: why should that offend, when they themselves had often sung it — Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles? Calvin makes the same argument turn on a question. How can unbelievers be qualified for praising God, who, though not entirely destitute of his mercy, are insensible of it and ignorant of his truth? It would serve no purpose for the prophet to address the heathen nations, unless they were to be gathered into the unity of the faith with the children of Abraham — and there is no ground for the censorious to refute Paul's reasoning by sophistry. He grants that the Spirit elsewhere calls on mountains, rivers, trees, rain and thunder to resound God's praises, since all creation silently proclaims him its Maker, but insists he is praised in a different manner by his rational creatures.

How far the call reaches Henry measures by what went before. For many ages in Judah only was God known, the sons of Levi and the seed of Israel praising him while the rest of the nations praised gods of wood and stone; and this call could not belong to Old Testament times, since it was not then given to any Gentile nation in a tongue they understood, nor were any of the people of the land admitted to praise God with Israel unless they became Jews and were circumcised. Spurgeon reads the same breadth as a rebuke: the psalm is clear proof that the Old Testament spirit differed widely from the narrow national bigotry with which the Jews of our Lord's day became so inveterately diseased, and it was an intimation to Israel that the grace of their God was not to be confined to one nation. Those already gathered out of every kindred, he adds, are but the advance-guard of a number no man can number.

Who is addressed Clarke divides between the clauses: let the Gentiles praise him, for he provides for their eternal salvation, and let the Jews praise him, for they have long been his peculiar people — since while God sends his Son to be a light to the Gentiles he sends him also to be the glory of Israel. Gill says the like from the other end: the Lord having chosen and Christ having redeemed some out of every kindred and tongue, and the Gospel being preached to all nations, they are excited to praise Jehovah, Father, Son and Spirit. Augustine takes the nations called here for the courts of the Lord's house and the true Jerusalem, and turns the verse against those who have refused to be children of that city, having cut themselves off from the communion of all nations.
2:
Both reasons given for the praise turn on words the commentators want to weigh. Gill would render the first that God's mercy prevailed over us, the verb being the one used of the waters of the flood prevailing over the earth, and he finds in that the exuberance of grace, its abounding and superabounding: there is an abundance of it in the heart of God, in his covenant and in his Son, displayed in redemption, in the forgiveness of sin, and in the conversion of sinners; and particularly there has been an inundation of it in the Gentile world, where it has flowed and overflowed, and where sin abounded grace has much more abounded. He is careful too about the us: not the Israelites only, of whom David was one, but the Gentiles also, since otherwise there would be no force in the reason why all nations should praise the Lord — the verse looking to the time when the two should be one people, partaking of the same grace and the same promises.

Clarke reads the same word as strength rather than bulk. It is not only great in number, he says, but powerful, prevailing over sin, Satan, death and hell. On the second reason he turns the abstraction into a list of things done: whatsoever God has promised, that he will most infallibly fulfil — he promised to send his Son into the world, and thus he has done; he promised that his Son should die for transgressors, and this he did; he promised to receive all who come to him through Christ Jesus, and this he invariably does; he promised that his Gospel should be preached in every nation, and this he is doing.

Keil and Delitzsch approach by way of the grammar and arrive at the same place. Even this shortest psalm has its peculiarities in point of language, the word used here for nations being otherwise alien to Old Testament Hebrew, which knows it only as an appellation of Ishmaelite or Midianite tribes; the two terms together mean all peoples without distinction and all nations without exception. The call is then confirmed twice over: from the might of the loving-kindness of Jahve, which proves itself mighty over Israel in that its intensity and fulness superabundantly cover human sin and infirmity — they compare Paul's word that where sin abounded grace did much more abound — and from his truth, by virtue of which history, running on into eternity, ends in a verifying of his promises. Mercy and truth, they conclude, are the two divine powers which shall one day be perfectly developed and displayed in Israel, and which, going forth from Israel, shall conquer the world.
